judgments.catchwords: LAND LAW — Forfeiture — Forfeiture for non-payment of quit rent — Application to compel decision on request for re-alienation — Whether State Authority under statutory duty to consider and communicate decision on application for re-alienation under s 133(3) National Land Code — Whether discretionary power under s 133(3) gives rise to enforceable public duty — Whether mandamus or mandatory injunction available to compel exercise of discretion — National Land Code, ss 133(3), 418 & 432 — Specific Relief Act 1950, s 44. LAND LAW — Forfeiture — Re-alienation of forfeited land — Petition for annulment previously refused — Subsequent request for re-alienation — Distinction between petition for annulment under ss 133(1) and (2) and discretionary power of re-alienation under s 133(3) — Whether former proprietor possesses legal right to determination of request for re-alienation — Nature and scope of State Authority’s discretionary power. ADMINISTRATIVE LAW — Mandamus — Public duty — Mandatory order compelling public authority to make decision — Whether statutory duty prerequisite to relief — Distinction between compelling performance of public duty and compelling exercise of discretionary power — Whether court may compel authority to entertain request where statute imposes no obligation to decide — Mandamus refused in absence of enforceable statutory duty. ADMINISTRATIVE LAW — Mandatory injunction — Section 44 Specific Relief Act 1950 — Mandatory order against public authority — Requirement that act sought to be compelled be clearly incumbent under law — Whether State Authority under legal obligation to determine application for re-alienation — Whether relief available in absence of statutory duty. ADMINISTRATIVE LAW — Judicial review — Public law proceedings — Appropriate mode of commencement — Whether application to compel exercise of statutory function should be commenced under O 53 Rules of Court 2012 or by Originating Summons — Court assuming procedural propriety without deciding issue where substantive claim failed for absence of legal duty. LAND LAW — National Land Code — Section 133 — Construction of statutory provisions — Petition for annulment — Re-alienation after forfeiture — Whether words “shall” in s 133(3) impose mandatory obligation to determine application for re-alienation — Whether mandatory language operates only upon prior decision to re-alienate — Purposive construction of statutory scheme. LAND LAW — Forfeiture — Functus officio — Previous application for annulment refused — Whether refusal exhausted State Authority’s jurisdiction — Effect of statutory provision preserving power to re-alienate “at any time” — Continuing existence of discretionary power distinguished from existence of enforceable duty. LAND LAW — Forfeiture — Limitation — Laches — Application seeking decision on request for re-alienation — Whether challenge directed at forfeiture or subsequent administrative inaction — Applicability of limitation periods under Public Authorities Protection Act 1948, O 53 Rules of Court 2012 and s 418 National Land Code — Whether doctrines of limitation and laches engaged. LAND LAW — Forfeiture — Service of statutory notices — Form 6A — Form 8A — Alleged defective substituted service — Notices allegedly affixed at adjoining property — Whether validity of service justiciable in proceedings seeking only order compelling decision — Whether challenge to validity of forfeiture confined to appeal under ss 134 and 418 National Land Code. PRACTICE AND PROCEDURE — Originating Summons — Relief against public authority — Mandatory order compelling exercise of statutory function — Affidavit evidence only — Whether disputed issues concerning validity of forfeiture and service of statutory notices capable of determination — Scope of proceedings confined to existence of enforceable statutory duty.

judgments.title: CHEAH TING FENG v LUMAYAN INDAH SDN BHD & ors
judgments.catchwords: Full trial - Plaintiff purchased 51 residential units for RM 110 million; Pleads fraudulent misrepresentation that he could use for short term rental; claims units constructed in material deviation from approved building plans and alleges breach of contract. - Plaintiff claims for recission, repayment of purchase price and damages; - Issues are whether there was any misrepresentation, any illegality arising out of non compliance with the building plans and breach of contract. - Court finds : a. no misrepresentation; b. the SPA's not rendered void by any alleged regulatory non compliance and that in any event, such non compliance has since been cured by the latest approved plans; c. there has been no material breach of contract as the Plaintiff received exactly what he inspected and bargained for; and d. the plaintiffs conduct estops him form pursuing recission. - Plaintiffs claim dismissed with costs.
judgments.judge: YA Dato' Anand Ponnudurai

judgments.title: SIVACHANDRAN A/L S JAYARAJAH v Pendakwa Raya
judgments.catchwords: Review jurisdiction - Rule 137 of the Rules of the Federal Court 1995 -Inherent powers of Federal Court – All sentences passed to be in accordance with the law – Avoiding miscarriage of justice - Exceptional circumstances - Fresh evidence of prisoner’s death following whipping. Constitutional Law - Federal Constitution - Articles 5(1), 8(1) and 8(2) Fundamental liberties - Life and personal liberty - Human dignity - Equal protection of the law - Whether it is in violation of medical ethics for medical officer to be participate in the execution of whipping. Judicial whipping - Corporal punishment - Whether judicial whipping amounts to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment (“CIDT”) - Whether punishment of whipping is inconsistent with constitutional protection of life, dignity and bodily integrity. Whether whipping is disproportionate and therefore contrary to Article 8(1) - Whether exemption of women from whipping constitutes prohibited discrimination on ground only of gender is contrary to Art 8(2) - Intelligible differentia. Whether whipping is against Art. 5 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (“UDHR”) and the ASEAN Human Rights Declaration in its prohibitions against CIDT - Whether whipping is against customary international law.

judgments.title: SA Coconut Enterprise v MOHD SAYUTI BIN SULAIMAN & ors
judgments.catchwords: Appeal from the Sessions Court – Principles on appellate intervention - Claim for goods sold and delivered – Sessions judge dismissed Plaintiff’s claim– Whether Plaintiff has legal capacity to sue – Plaintiff commenced suit in its business name and not in the name of proprietor – Plaintiff is a sole proprietorship business – Action ought to have been commenced in the proprietor’s name – Whether there is a contractual or business relationship between Plaintiff and Defendant - Burden is on Plaintiff under Sections 101 and 102 of the Evidence Act 1950 to prove its case – No Purchase Orders issued by Defendant to Plaintiff – No Delivery Orders issued by Plaintiff to Defendant – Incumbent upon Plaintiff to lead evidence to prove Defendant ordered and took delivery – Plaintiff failed to call witnesses from Port Authority or lorry drivers or transporter – No evidence that payments deposited into Plaintiff’s bank account were for Defendant – Plaintiff had contractual relationship with which business entity in respect of the coconuts sold and delivered – No receipt produced by Plaintiff – Payment vouchers become an important piece of document evidencing payments from a payee – Payments were from a different entity than the Defendant – Failure of Plaintiff to adduce evidence of the non-existence of MJ Transport invites an adverse inference to be made according to section 114(g) Evidence Act 1950 – Sessions judge had considered all documentary and oral evidence
